:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 


$$
M= \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -12 & 4\end{array}\right].
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -12 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-3y &=1 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 3y = 1.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=1+3y,$ and the general solution is



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1+3y \\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$



where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1+3y \\ y\end{bmatrix}=⟨1+3y,\,y⟩,\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 \\ -3 & 3 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 \\ -3 & 3 & -9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y &=3 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x-y=3.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=3+y,$ and the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=3+y \\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3+y \\ y\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -12 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-3y &=1 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 3y = 1.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=1+3y,$ and the general solution is



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1+3y \\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$



where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1+3y \\ y\end{bmatrix}=⟨1+3y,\,y⟩,\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+5y &=4 \\ 4x+10y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$


Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:



$$
M = \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 10 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$



Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 10 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{5}{2} & 2 \\ 4 & 10 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{5}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+\frac{5}{2}y &=2 \\ 0x+0y &=-8.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



However, the final equation $0x+0y=-8$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=-8,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's consider a system of linear equations where the corresponding coefficient matrix is singular. For example, consider the following system and its associated augmented matrix:


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=-5 \\ -3x+6y &=15\end{aligned}\right. \qquad M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & -5 \\ -3 & 6 & 15\end{array} \right]
$$



To solve the system, we can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as usual. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -5 \\ -3 & 6 & 15\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=-5 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 2y = -5.
$$

Finally, we describe the **general solution** of our system.

- The first variable in our equation, $x,$ is called a **basic variable**.

- The second variable in our equation, $y,$ is called a **free variable**.

Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x = -5+2y.$ So the general solution of the system is


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-5+2y \\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$


where the free variable $y$ is any number.

In vector form, this solution is written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5+2y \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+y\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is the equation of a straight line on a plane. Any point on this line satisfies our system of equations.

If we want to find some **particular solution** of the system, we simply choose some particular value of $y$ and find the corresponding value of $x$ on the line. For example, if we choose $y=0,$ then the corresponding value is $x=-5$ and the particular solution is $x=-5,$ $y=0.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a Singular 2x2 System of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Given a $2 \times 2$ system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:

- The system has exactly *one solution* if and only if the respective coefficient matrix is non-singular (meaning that the determinant is not zero). Such systems are called **consistent independent**.

- The system has *infinitely many solutions* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s. These systems are called **consistent dependent**.

- The system has *no solution* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s on the left-hand side and a non-zero element on the right-hand side. These are called **inconsistent** systems.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

**Note:** A system of linear equations of the form 


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}ax+by &=0 \\ cx+dy &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$


where we have only $0$'s on the right-hand side, is called **homogeneous**. A homogeneous system always has at least one solution, namely, the solution $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle 0,0 \rangle.$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: The Number of Solutions of a 2x2 System

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Sometimes, a system of equations might not have any solutions. For example, consider the following augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 10\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=3 \\ 0x+0y &=10.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



The final equation, $0x+0y=10,$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=10,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=
  \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & -8\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & -8\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -8 & -8\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{8}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=0 \\ y &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=1$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+2(1)=0 
	\quad\Rightarrow\quad
	x=-2.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-2$ and $y=1.$ Or, in vector form, $\left<  -2,1 \right>.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-x+5y &=5 \\ x-6y &=5.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=
	\left[
	\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 5 & 5 \\ 1 & -6 & 5\end{array}
	\right].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 5 & 5 \\ 1 & -6 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -5 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -5 & -5 \\ 0 & -1 & 10\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -5 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-5y &=-5 \\ y &=-10,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-10$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x-5(-10)=-5 
	\quad\Rightarrow\quad
	x=-55.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-55$ and $y=-10.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -55,-10 \rangle.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Show that the following system of equations has no solution.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x + 2y &=4 \\ 2x + y &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's start by solving the system using elimination.

Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-2$, then we will get a $-4x$ term that can cancel with the $4x$ term in the first equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y &=4 \\ 2x+y &=4 && \text{multiply by } -2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

When we add the two equations, it turns out that both variables cancel, and we obtain a false statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4x + 2y &= 4 \\
- 4x - 2y &= -8 \\
0 &= (4 - 8) \\
0 &= -4
\end{aligned}
$$

The statement $0=-4$ is *always false*. Therefore, we conclude that the system has *no solutions*.

Geometrically, this means that the corresponding lines *do not intersect*. In other words, they are *parallel.*

![](images/04/048c377f99093f493c37bc4de0363527996c8928348b43ad9c9747965f984c1f.png)

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
At how many points do the following lines intersect?

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - 2y &= 2 \\[6pt]
10y - 5x &= -10
\end{aligned}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The number of points of intersection between the two lines is equal to the number of solutions of the corresponding system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x - 2y &=2 \\ 10y - 5x &=-10\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve the system using substitution. First, we solve for $x$ in the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - 2y &= 2 \\
x &= 2y + 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute

$$
x=2y+2
$$

into the second equation and solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
10y - 5x &= -10 \\
10y - 5(2y + 2) &= -10 \\
10y - 10y - 10 &= -10 \\
- 10 &= -10
\end{aligned}
$$

The result is a statement that's always true. Therefore, we conclude that the system has infinitely many solutions.

Consequently, the lines intersect at infinitely many points (i.e., they coincide).

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Number of Intersection Points of Two Lines

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find all points of intersection of the following lines:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x+2y &= 2 \\[6pt]
6x+4y &= 4
\end{aligned}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The points of intersection of the lines correspond to the solutions of the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x + 2y &=2 \\ 6x + 4y &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve the system using elimination. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-2$, then we will get a $-6x$ term that can cancel with the $6x$ term in the second equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+2y &=2 && \text{multiply by } -2 \\ 6x+4y &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

When we add the two equations, it turns out that both variables cancel, and we obtain a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-6x - 4y &= -4 \\
6x + 4y &= 4 \\
0 &= (-4 + 4) \\
0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the lines have infinitely many intersection points.

We want to find an expression that represents every solution to the system. Any value of $x$ is a solution, and we can find the corresponding $y$-coordinate for each $x$-coordinate by solving one of the lines for $y$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x + 2y &= 2 \\
2y &= 2 - 3x \\
y &= \frac{2 - 3x}{2} \\
y &= 1 - \frac{3}{2}x
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points of intersection are

$$
\left(x,1-\dfrac{3}{2}x \right)
$$

where $x$ is any number.
